newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Stg seen down to 2.40 marks by end-year.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Stg seen down to 2.40 marks by end-year.

text.p: Sterling's rally over recent weeks cannot be sustained and by the end of this year the pound is expected to drop back against the mark as markets price in political worries, according to a Reuters survey of economists.

By end-1996 sterling is expected to fall back to around 2.4000 marks after touching a 21-month high at 2.4475 marks on Wednesday, the mean forecast of 21 economists showed. After the general election, due by May 1997, sterling is expected to drop further to around 2.3750 marks.
The highest sterling forecast for end-1996 was 2.4800 marks and the lowest was 2.2800 marks. The range for mid-1997 was 2.1000 marks to 2.5500 marks.
"Political worries will start to mount in the next quarter and we don't think a Labour government has been priced into the market," Philip Uglow, economist at Union Discount said.

A major reason for sterling's climb is investors looking for yield and an alternative to the Swiss franc, where traditionally capital has flowed when there are uncertainties connected with the German mark or the dollar, analysts said.
"Sterling has been pushed up to these levels on EMU convergence trades, but as we move on through the year we may see some of those trades being taken off and the pound will be sold," Uglow said.
Economists were also asked for expectations for sterling/dollar. By end-1996 cable is expected on average at 1.5580 and slightly lower at 1.5510 by end-June from 1.5840 on Wednesday.

If, as opinion polls suggest, the opposition Labour party wins the election, uncertainties over policies will add to negative sentiment for sterling versus the mark in the first half of 1997, analysts said.
Analysts expect the dollar to fall back next year and there will as usual be a ripple effect for sterling which normally shadows the dollar.
James McKay, UK economist at Paine Webber also expects a pick-up in the German economy to contribute to sterling losses versus the mark next year.

"While the Bundesbank is keeping the dollar buoyed with verbal rhetoric at the moment, next year as the German economy begins to recover, sterling will run out of ammunition," he said. But a minority of the economists in the survey expected sterling to be at higher levels versus the mark by end-1996.

"The latest data is aligned to fears that the next move in UK interest rates is up, oil prices look as if they will continue to firm and sterling will continue to benefit from its petro-currency status," Nick Stamenkovic economist at DKB International said.
Benchmark Brent crude oil prices hit five-year highs on Tuesday on concerns of low U.S. heating oil stocks. The November contract traded up to its high of $25.06 per barrel.
Five of the economists surveyed expect sterling to continue to rally into next year and trade at higher levels.
"With continental Europe in the doldrums through aggressive fiscal tightening, the medium term outlook is pretty positive," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America.
David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns in London, also cites the converging policies of the two main parties for his positive view of sterling prospects.

"Once the election is out of the way and Labour is in, City worries will prove unfounded. The Conservatives have moved to centre-ground as has Labour. The two parties are almost indistinguishable," Brown said.
